title: Why the good suffer
hookLine: the king asks why good people suffer; Nagasena answers carefully

cards: The king has heard the mango and the milk: deeds bear fruit. So he takes the idea to its edge, where it hurts. The Buddha, he says, had cleared away every unwholesome deed.
Then why, in the stories, did he ever suffer? Why did a splinter of rock wound his foot? Why was he ever sick?
If every pain is the fruit of something done, the king says, then either the Buddha had bad deeds left, or the teaching is wrong. Pick one.
It's a question heard in hospital waiting rooms too: why did this happen to someone who didn't deserve it?

teach.h: NOT EVERY PAIN HAS KAMMA AS ITS ROOT.
teach.b: First, the careful answer. Nagasena won't pick either. The mistake, he says, is in the premise: not everything that is felt has kamma as its root.

teach.h: THE BODY, THE SEASONS, A BLOW, KAMMA.
teach.b: Pain can come from several causes: from the body's own workings, what the old medicine called wind, bile and phlegm; from the change of seasons; from careless treatment; from a sudden blow from outside; and from kamma.
Kamma is one cause among them, not the only one. Those who say every pain is the result of past deeds, he says, go too far.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA'S FOOT: PAIN, NOT PAYMENT.
teach.b: Third, the Buddha's foot. The splinter of rock was not the ripening of some old deed. It came from someone else's act and the plain fact of a stone breaking.
The Buddha felt the pain. That did not mean he had earned it. Fourth, why this matters on an ordinary day.
It's easy to hear the teaching on kamma as a verdict: you're sick, so you must have done something. Nagasena refuses that reading, in a book the tradition keeps.
When someone is suffering, the question of what they did to deserve it may have no answer at all, because the suffering may not have come from anything they did. Bodies fail. Weather turns.

teach.h: ROOM FOR HELP, NOT A VERDICT.
teach.b: That leaves room for something besides judgment: room to sit beside the person, and to help.
The king asked the hard question at full strength, and Nagasena answered without pretending it was easier than it was.

how: Buddhist teachers point to this passage of the Questions of King Milinda to say that not all suffering is the result of past kamma, and that illness and accident have other causes too.

o: action, deed: one cause of pain among several
a penalty handed down for every pain you feel
fate: everything that happens was set for you

games.q: why the good suffer: tap the pairs.
p: why did the Buddha ever suffer?
not every pain has kamma as its root
pain, but not the fruit of old deeds
the body's own causes of pain

s: Nagasena teaches that every pain is the result of past deeds
he says those who claim that go too far: kamma is one cause among several.
in the dialogue, the Buddha's wounded foot was not the ripening of old kamma
Nagasena says it came from another's act and a stone breaking.
the king's question is treated as disrespectful and refused
Nagasena answers it at full strength.

games.q: you're Nagasena. the king says: if every pain is the fruit of deeds, either the Buddha had bad deeds left, or the teaching is wrong. pick one.
o: the Buddha must have had bad deeds left.
the teaching on kamma is wrong.
neither: not every pain comes from kamma.
games.why: he rejects the premise. pain can come from the body, the seasons, careless treatment, a blow from outside, or kamma: one cause among several.

practice: Bring to mind something that happened to someone, maybe you, that nobody deserved. You don't need to explain it or fix it; if a judgment comes, they must have, I must have, notice it and set it down.
Breathe beside it, the way you might sit beside a friend.

wordCard.voice: Kamma. One cause of pain among several, Nagasena says, not the whole story, and not always the reason someone suffers.

orig.note: Pali: action, deed (Sanskrit karma). in this dialogue, one cause of pain among several, not the only one.

carryVoice: Your line: the hard question. Some pain asks for help, not a verdict. See you tomorrow.
